entities.name: Donatus Magnus
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Donatus Magnus, also known as Donatus of Carthage, rose to prominence in the early fourth century CE as the charismatic and prophetic leader of the Donatist movement, a distinctive Christian sect that profoundly fractured the Church in North Africa for over a century. His emergence around 313 CE, following the devastating Diocletianic Persecution, centered on a rigorous demand for clerical purity and a rejection of any clergy who had compromised their faith during the persecutions, thereby challenging the burgeoning authority of the Roman imperial Church under Constantine I.

The core of the Donatist dispute ignited with the contested election of Caecilian as Bishop of Carthage around 311 CE, whom Donatus and his followers accused of being consecrated by a "traditor" (one who had surrendered sacred texts to Roman authorities). Donatus was subsequently elected as a rival bishop, asserting that sacraments administered by morally impure clergy were invalid and necessitating re-baptism for those joining the Donatist communion. This uncompromising stance led to repeated imperial interventions, including the Council of Arles in 314 CE and subsequent decrees by Constantine I, all of which condemned Donatism and initiated periods of persecution against its adherents. Donatus himself was exiled multiple times, notably in 347 CE by Emperor Constans, and died in exile around 355 CE.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Donatus Magnus's leadership initiated a major schism that deeply divided North African Christianity for over a century, compelling significant theological developments within the broader Catholic Church, particularly through the writings of Augustine of Hippo. The movement demonstrated the enduring power of local religious identity against imperial ecclesiastical uniformity.
